reasons: Lake identity record lists input case name United States v. Xiang, court 8th Cir. 2023, date_decided 2023-05-05, and docket 22-1801.
Lake citations record lists official citation 67 F.4th 895; the opinion text caption and filing date match the case identity.
The opinion states the principal issue was the warrantless seizure and forensic search of Xiang's digital devices as he was leaving the country under the Fourth Amendment border-search exception.
The court's analysis turns on whether the outbound electronic-device search was a border search and what suspicion standard applied, supporting the Border Searches home role.
residual_risks: No separate Border Searches home-page taxonomy was disclosed, so the 'Key' role is supported from the case centrality shown in the opinion text.

defect.evidence_quote: we need not decide today whether reasonable suspicion is required for an advanced or forensic border search of electronic devices
defect.locator_note: text/United States v. Xiang__0262ad.txt, Motion to Suppress Issues section, slip page 8
defect.problem: The holding overclaims that the Eighth Circuit adopted a rule requiring reasonable, individualized suspicion for non-routine forensic device searches. The opinion says that standard is appropriate but expressly reserves whether reasonable suspicion is required because the officers had it here.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: The border-search exception applied to Xiang's outbound devices; the court treated reasonable, individualized suspicion for advanced forensic device searches as an appropriate standard but did not decide whether it is required, because CBP had reasonable suspicion on these facts, so suppression was properly denied.

reasons: The outbound-border-search portion is supported by the opinion's statement that the exception applies with equal force to persons or objects leaving the country.
The denial of suppression is supported: the court agreed CBP had reasonable suspicion and affirmed.
The asserted categorical adoption of a required reasonable-suspicion standard is contradicted by the court's express reservation of that question.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Avoid saying the court 'adopted' or 'held' the reasonable-suspicion requirement; say it applied or assumed that standard and found it satisfied.
